scenarios.title: The First-Time Leader
scenarios.subtitle: Authority without micromanaging
scenarios.description: A respected peer becomes team lead, but expectations are unclear and an employee questions the sudden change in authority.
scenarios.briefing: You have just been selected to lead a six-person service improvement team. Until Friday you were a peer. On Monday you inherit a missed deadline, an informal decision-making culture, and confusion about your new authority. Senior leadership expects results, but the team expects you to keep working like one of them. There is no single correct leadership style; your challenge is to adapt without abandoning fairness, transparency, or accountability.
scenarios.mission: Set the standard for trustworthy leadership: clarify roles, listen, establish accountability, and demonstrate consistent judgment.
stakes: Clarity of expectations and decision rights
Fairness and credibility of a new leader

moments.behavior: Jordan interrupts your opening team meeting: “Yesterday you were one of us. Now you are telling us how to do our jobs?” Two coworkers glance down and stop talking.
moments.context: The team is watching how you handle respectful disagreement and your new role.
moments.cues: Defensiveness, ambiguity about authority, a risk to trust.
moments.question: How will you assert leadership without humiliating a former peer?

options.reaction: “Understood.”

scenarios.subtitle: Balance the task and the relationship
scenarios.description: A high-volume team is falling behind while an excellent employee quietly approaches burnout.

scenarios.mission: Adapt your leadership style to the needs of the people and the task: clarify the work, address overload, and preserve performance.
stakes: Deliverable due in ten business days

scenarios.subtitle: Strengths, triggers, and difficult conversations
scenarios.description: Two talented colleagues clash over how to work, and their strengths are becoming sources of friction.
scenarios.briefing: Your project team is divided. Sofia moves quickly and pushes for decisions; Daniel checks details and raises risk concerns. Both care about delivering high-quality work. stakes: A partnership between two strong contributors

moments.title: The failed test
moments.behavior: Omar says: “I have let everyone down. We should just scrap the whole project.” Grace disagrees and shows a specific unresolved failure.
moments.context: A setback is real, but its scope and cause are not yet known.
moments.cues: Stress response; premature judgment; useful evidence.
moments.question: How will you respond to Omar and the team?
moments.verify: Conduct a bounded risk assessment and confirm the failure scope before the go/no-go decision.

options.action: “We will examine what failed and who is affected. Omar, your job is to help us understand the test, not carry the setback alone.”
options.reaction: “I can walk everyone through the failure logs.”
options.signal: Omar resumes contributing, and the team separates facts from emotions.
options.lesson: Calm leadership keeps accountability and learning in balance.

options.action: “It probably means nothing. Let us launch as planned.”
options.reaction: “But the test showed a real service failure.”
options.signal: Known risks remain unaddressed.
options.lesson: Optimism cannot replace evidence.

options.action: “Omar is right; the project is a disaster. Cancel everything.”
options.reaction: “Should we at least review the findings?”
options.signal: A major decision is made without diagnosis.
options.lesson: Stress can narrow judgment prematurely.

moments.title: A tempting workaround
moments.behavior: Ben proposes an untested workaround to meet the launch date. Grace argues it may disadvantage customers with assistive needs.
moments.context: A fast solution may create a new problem.
moments.cues: Unintended consequences and inclusion.
moments.question: What decision process will you use?
moments.verify: Document the decision, safeguards, owner, and next review time.

options.action: “I cannot make this call until everyone agrees completely.”
options.reaction: “The sponsor needs an answer by five.”
options.signal: Delay becomes an unexamined decision with consequences.
options.lesson: Seek input, then own a reasoned decision.

options.action: “Ben is confident. Let us trust his judgment and ship it today.”
options.reaction: “But we have not tested accessibility.”
options.signal: A serious known uncertainty is ignored.
options.lesson: Confidence does not remove the need to verify risk.

options.action: “We will test the workaround against customer impact and stop conditions, then compare a limited rollout with a short delay.”
options.reaction: “That gives us a fair way to choose.”
options.signal: The team evaluates credible alternatives rather than defending camps.
options.lesson: Under uncertainty, leaders can use bounded tests and decision criteria.

moments.title: Communicating the setback
moments.behavior: Nadia asks what to tell leadership. The team wants to avoid looking incompetent. You have a preliminary cause analysis and two credible options.
moments.context: Communication must distinguish preliminary assessment from confirmed fact.
moments.cues: Honesty, decisiveness, and learning orientation.
moments.question: How do you brief the sponsor?
moments.verify: After the decision, debrief the setback, test mitigations, and capture lessons for the next launch.

options.action: “Everything will be fine; we are confident the workaround solves it.”
options.reaction: “What testing supports that?”
options.signal: Unsupported certainty undermines confidence.
options.lesson: Confidence should match the evidence.

options.action: “Here is what the test showed, what remains uncertain, two options with tradeoffs, and my recommendation with the next verification point.”
options.reaction: “That is the decision-quality briefing I need.”
options.signal: The sponsor can act confidently without being misled.
options.lesson: Clear judgment makes uncertainty actionable.

options.action: “It is all someone else’s fault, so there is nothing for us to do.”
options.reaction: “I still need a plan.”
options.signal: Ownership and action disappear behind blame.
options.lesson: Leaders accept responsibility for the response even when causes are shared.
